newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee nations vow flexibility as prices soar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee nations vow flexibility as prices soar.

text.p: A spiral in world coffee prices that threatens a consumer backlash led producing nations to decide at London talks on Monday that they should try to be more flexible in matching supply to demand.

The worry within the Association of Coffee Producing Countries is that the speculative bubble in coffee - one U.S. futures contract hit a 20-year high last week - may erode demand for the beverage, as people drink more tea or soft drinks instead.

Even as the exporters met, Americans were hit with a new hike on coffee at the check-out when Folgers, a leading retailer, passed on some of the 1997 rise in the world price of green (unroasted) beans by raising its 13-ounce can 30 cents to $3.36.

A volatile mix of factors - low stocks, tight supply from Colombia and fears that Brazil, the biggest exporter, may have another frost - has lured speculators to the futures markets and set off the longest unbroken rally in coffee in two decades..
Last week saw U.S. spot May futures for better-quality arabica beans trade at $2.80 per pound, the highest since 1977.
The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC), now meeting in London, accounts for about 75 percent of world output.
Quota rules aim to cap its exports at 25.5 million bags in the first half of 1997 but it has to decide policy for beyond June 30.
Delegates said that a six-nation technical group that included Brazil had come up with a draft proposal to submit to a full conference on Wednesday.
ACPC president Rubens Barbosa would not disclose details but a delegation source said that the group would be looking to retain quotas but with "flexibility in the allocation".
The market was short of specific types of coffee "so we are starting on how to discuss the flexibility of what the market is wanting right now...that is the main idea".
Market analysts say that any move may be mostly symbolic because, at curent prices, nobody is expected to honour quotas.
"It is hard to think of one producing country which is even thinking about adhering to its quota...market mechanisms have superseded any kind of export restraint..." say brokers GNI Ltd.
London futures for robusta coffee beans extended the rally on Monday. The July contract rose $135 to $2,190 per tonne before easing slightly.
New York's most representative arabica contract, also for July, eased below $2.45 per pound on profit-taking but remained about double where it began 1997.
Monday's retail price rise by Procter & Gamble unit Folgers Coffee Co is its fourth this year. The total of these increases adds up to almost 50 percent.
"The price of Folgers coffee generally reflects the price of green coffee sold on the commodity market," it said.

"Green coffee prices have been rising since January...due to a number of factors including reduced crop estimates for the upcoming coffee harvest in Brazil, reduced availability of coffee from Central America and Colombia, and generally tight supply of arabica beans..."
Among European roasters (processors) French Cafes Excella SA, which plans new retail prices rises in June, says it doubts whether futures really reflect supply/demand fundamentals.
"There is no risk of a coffee shortage. We are being held hostage by a speculative game..." Marketing Director Jean-Jacques Dothee said last Friday.
Dothee also gave a warning that high prices might scare away consumers, notably young people switching to soft drinks.
